source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"First-degree frostbite, a superficial injury that does not form blisters after tissue rewarming","B":"Second-degree frostbite, which develops clear or milky blisters after the tissue has been rewarmed","C":"Third-degree frostbite, which causes deeper injury and typically forms hemorrhagic blisters","D":"Fourth-degree frostbite, which extends into deeper structures such as muscle, tendon, or bone"}}
source_row.rationale: Traditional frostbite grading is assessed after rewarming. First-degree injury is superficial and does not produce blisters; clear or milky blisters indicate second-degree injury, while hemorrhagic blisters or deeper tissue involvement indicate more severe frostbite.
source_row.source_detail: Frostbite grading after rewarming: first degree has no blisters; second degree clear/milky blisters; deeper grades have hemorrhagic/deep injury; reviewed 2026-08-14.
source_row.source_name: Wilderness Medical Society — Frostbite Classification and Staging
source_row.stem: After rewarming, a client with frostbite has erythematous, mildly edematous skin without blister formation or deeper tissue injury. How is this injury best classified?
